metadata.title: Students’ 2018 PISA reading self-concept: Identifying predictors and examining model generalizability for emergent bilinguals

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2018 PISA reading assessment data for the United States, with students nested within schools (and teacher/school context variables). The authors report including student sampling weights (scaled) in each analysis and centering at Level 1 using cluster means and at Level 2 using the grand mean. For the multilevel modeling (MLM) stage, they also include replication weights to account for between-cluster variance (e.g., schools), following PISA recommendations. The paper does not describe any additional weight variable names (e.g., specific W_FSTUWT codes), but it explicitly states that sampling weights and replication weights were used, so estimates are intended to reflect PISA’s complex sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full available 2018 PISA reading assessment sample for the United States (15-year-olds), with a total of 4,838 students participating in the reading assessment. For variable inclusion, the authors applied a 20% missingness cutoff to exclude predictors with missing data rates beyond 20%. For the Elastic Net (ENET) variable selection stage, missing values in the retained variables were imputed using predictive mean matching (PMM) via the R mice package. For the subsequent two-level multilevel modeling (MLM), missing data were handled using a two-level fully conditional specification (FCS) imputation approach implemented with mice/miceadds.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Trying hard helps get a good job

top_predictors: Perceived information and communications technologies competence
Availability and usage of information and communications technologies
main_findings.performance_metrics: Elastic Net variable selection (no predictive accuracy reported). Multilevel modeling full model: LRT=15.11 (df=1, p<0.001); L1 R square=0.14; L2 R square=0.16. Significant fixed effects include reading habits (β=0.204, SE=0.014, p<0.001), perceived ICT competence (β=0.153, SE=0.016, p<0.001), work mastery (β=0.102, SE=0.016, p<0.001), teacher understanding (β=0.089, SE=0.017, p<0.001), and availability/usage of ICT (β=-0.081, SE=0.025, p=0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (United States, student/teacher/school context) the study leveraged reading habits, perceived ICT competence, work mastery, teacher understanding, and availability/usage of ICT to predict students’ reading self-concept, finding that reading habits, ICT competence, work mastery, and teacher understanding were positive predictors while ICT availability/usage was a negative predictor. This indicates that strengthening students’ reading routines, mastery-oriented persistence, and teachers’ understanding—along with supporting productive ICT competence rather than mere outside-of-school ICT use—may improve reading self-concept, though the correlational design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (United States, emergent bilinguals subset)
top_predictors: Perceived information and communications technologies competence
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel modeling full model (emergent bilinguals): adjusted ICC between schools=0.10; conditional ICC between schools=0.09. Significant predictors reported in Table 6 include perceived ICT competence (β=0.150, SE=0.017, p<0.001), work mastery (β=0.102, SE=0.018, p=0.004), reading habits (β=0.072, SE=0.036, p=0.049), teacher understanding (β=0.087, SE=0.018, p=0.020), and physical education in teacher training (β=-0.321, SE=0.145, p=0.030).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for the emergent bilinguals subset in the United States, the study leveraged perceived ICT competence, work mastery, reading habits, teacher understanding, and physical education in teacher training to predict reading self-concept, finding that ICT competence, mastery, reading habits, and teacher understanding were positive predictors while physical education in teacher training was a negative predictor. This indicates that emergent bilinguals’ reading self-concept may be especially sensitive to mastery-oriented supports, teacher understanding, and ICT competence development, suggesting targeted instructional and professional-development priorities for this group, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (United States, native English speakers subset)
top_predictors: Perceived information and communications technologies competence
Hosting visiting teachers from other countries
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel modeling full model (native English speakers): adjusted ICC between schools=0.01; conditional ICC between schools=0.008. Significant predictors in Table 6 include availability/usage of ICT (β=-0.100, SE=0.028, p<0.001), teacher understanding (β=0.087, SE=0.018, p<0.001), work mastery (β=0.102, SE=0.018, p<0.001), perceived ICT competence (β=0.150, SE=0.017, p<0.001), reading habits (β=0.235, SE=0.016, p<0.001), and hosting visiting teachers from other countries (β=-0.088, SE=0.040, p=0.032).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for native English speakers in the United States, the study leveraged reading habits, perceived ICT competence, work mastery, teacher understanding, and hosting visiting teachers from other countries to predict reading self-concept, finding that reading habits, ICT competence, mastery, and teacher understanding were positive predictors while outside-of-school ICT availability/usage and hosting visiting teachers were negative predictors. This indicates that interventions to improve reading self-concept for native English speakers may focus on sustaining reading routines and mastery goals while carefully managing how ICT is used outside school, though the findings remain correlational and may reflect unmeasured contextual differences.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Reading data from the United States (N=4,838 students; 164 schools) to identify predictors of students’ reading self-concept, defined by three self-report items (“I am a good reader,” “I am able to understand difficult texts,” “I read fluently”). The authors first use Elastic Net for variable selection across student, teacher, and school levels, then estimate two-level multilevel models (with replication weights) to test relative contributions for the full sample and for emergent bilinguals (N=736) versus native English speakers (N=4,054). In the full model, reading habits, teacher understanding, work mastery, and perceived ICT competence were significant positive predictors, while availability/usage of ICT and subjective well-being were significant negative predictors; model fit is summarized by LRT and R² at levels 1 and 2. The paper does not report predictive accuracy metrics for Elastic Net, and the outcomes are self-concept measures, so results are correlational rather than causal.
